title: 07 — Databricks SQL, Compute and Performance
html:
07 — Databricks SQL, Compute and Performance

The one idea: compute is disposable and billed by the second, so choose the smallest kind that does the job, let the platform maintain table layout, and define business metrics once. Speed comes from reading less (layout, pruning, caching), not from bigger clusters.

1. What it is

The compute side of Databricks, and the features that make SQL fast and consistent:

  • Compute types: classic clusters, serverless compute for notebooks and jobs, and SQL warehouses (classic, pro, serverless).
  • Photon: the vectorised C++ execution engine behind Databricks SQL and many runtimes.
  • Predictive optimization: automatic OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and statistics for UC managed tables.
  • Liquid clustering: flexible data layout that replaces fixed partitioning and Z-ordering.
  • Lakehouse Federation: query external databases through UC.
  • Metric views: the semantic layer.
  • AI/BI: dashboards and Genie, natural-language questions over governed data.

2. Why it matters

  • Cost: a warehouse that never auto-stops, or a cluster sized for the worst day, is most of a bill.
  • Consistency: two dashboards computing AUM two ways is a governance failure. Metric views fix it.
  • Reach: federation lets you query a SQL Server or PostgreSQL source in place while you decide whether to ingest it.

3. The main ideas

3.1 Choosing compute

Need Choose Why
BI and SQL dashboards Serverless SQL warehouse Starts in seconds, scales with load, auto-stops
Scheduled pipelines and jobs Serverless jobs compute, or job clusters Pay per run. Nothing idle
Interactive data science, GPUs Classic all-purpose cluster with a policy Libraries, GPUs, long sessions
Cheap learning Free Edition Serverless only, one 2X-Small warehouse, five concurrent job tasks, daily quota (per the docs, checked 2026-10-26)

A third-party guide reports that Intelligent Workload Management on serverless SQL warehouses predicts each query's compute needs. Databricks reported in 2025 that Predictive Query Execution and Photon vectorised shuffle made serverless queries up to 25% faster.

3.2 Layout: liquid clustering and predictive optimization

  • Liquid clustering (CLUSTER BY (col, ...)) groups related rows into the same files incrementally. You can change the clustering keys later without rewriting everything. CLUSTER BY AUTO lets the platform pick the keys.
  • Predictive optimization runs maintenance (OPTIMIZE, VACUUM, statistics) on UC managed tables when the platform predicts it pays off. A July 2026 report notes that upgrading external tables to managed tables brings predictive optimization along. This is one more reason to prefer managed tables.

3.3 Lakehouse Federation

Two forms:

  • Query federation: a UC connection plus a foreign catalog lets you run SQL against MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Snowflake, Redshift and others. UC governs it, and queries are pushed down where possible.
  • Catalog federation: UC reads the catalog of another metastore (for example Hive or Glue) and governs those tables as foreign tables.

Use federation to explore, and for small reference lookups. Ingest (Lakeflow Connect) when you need history, heavy joins, or independence from the source's load.

3.4 Metric views

Measures and dimensions are declared once in YAML, with CREATE VIEW ... WITH METRICS LANGUAGE YAML AS $$ ... $$, and queried with MEASURE(name):

-- Not run. YAML keys differ between doc versions (for example dimensions: vs fields:). Check the YAML reference.
SELECT category, MEASURE(total_aum_cr) FROM gold.fund_metrics GROUP BY category;

They need Runtime 16.4 or above. One source dates GA to April 2026, but parts of the reference still show Public Preview, so check before use.

3.5 Reading a query profile

Check these in order:

  1. Files and bytes read versus pruned: layout problem?
  2. Spill to disk: memory pressure, a skewed join?
  3. Shuffle size: a join or aggregation on the wrong key?
  4. Photon coverage: did any operator fall back?
  5. Result cache hits: repeated dashboards should hit it.

4. Working code

This chapter has no runnable code, because the features need a workspace. The SQL is not run:

-- Not run.
CREATE TABLE fin.silver.fund_nav (isin STRING, nav_date DATE, nav DECIMAL(18,4))
CLUSTER BY (nav_date, isin);

ALTER TABLE fin.silver.fund_nav CLUSTER BY AUTO;           -- let the platform pick keys

CREATE CONNECTION pg_ops TYPE postgresql
OPTIONS (host 'ops-db.internal', port '5432', user secret('ops', 'user'), password secret('ops', 'pwd'));
CREATE FOREIGN CATALOG ops USING CONNECTION pg_ops OPTIONS (database 'operations');
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ops.public.scheme_master;              -- governed, pushed down where possible

SELECT usage_date, sku_name, SUM(usage_quantity) AS dbus      -- what did compute cost last week?
FROM system.billing.usage
WHERE usage_date >= current_date() - INTERVAL 7 DAYS
GROUP BY ALL ORDER BY usage_date;

The CREATE CONNECTION options differ by database type and change between releases. Copy them from the federation docs for your source.

5. Common mistakes

  1. All-purpose clusters for scheduled jobs. They cost more, and stay up after the job ends.
  2. Over-partitioning. Many tiny partitions mean many tiny files. Use liquid clustering.
  3. Federating heavy production joins. You load the source system and lose history. Ingest instead.
  4. No auto-stop on warehouses. Idle cost adds up quickly.
  5. Metrics defined in every dashboard. Use metric views, so a number means one thing everywhere.

6. Exercise (1 hour)

On Free Edition: create a clustered table, load a few million made-up rows with range(), then run the same filter before and after OPTIMIZE. Compare files read in the query profile. Then query system.billing.usage, if your workspace exposes it.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. Which compute would you pick for a nightly pipeline, and why?
  2. What does predictive optimization do, and on which tables?
  3. When is Lakehouse Federation the wrong choice?
  4. Why does liquid clustering beat fixed partitioning for most tables?
  5. What are the first two things to check in a slow query profile?

Answers

  1. Serverless jobs compute or a job cluster: billed per run, with nothing idle.
  2. It runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and statistics automatically on Unity Catalog managed tables.
  3. For heavy, repeated joins, or when you need history. Ingest the data instead.
  4. Keys can change without a full rewrite, it adapts to skew, and it avoids tiny partitions.
  5. Bytes read versus pruned, and spill.

8. Sources
